💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester United lost 4-0 at Liverpool in their opening match under Mauricio Pochettino.
  • Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for fresh head coach Mauricio Pochettino.
  • The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United lost 4-0 at Liverpool in their opening match under Mauricio Pochettino.

Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for fresh head coach Mauricio Pochettino.

The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.

But Pochettino did not look like a man without pressure after 15 minutes of what turned into a 4-0 defeat.

By that point, his side were already 2-0 behind and down to 10 men. Liverpool's fans were gleefully singing about the Argentine being "sacked in the morning", even though he was only a sixth of the way through his first game in charge.

A day later, United supporters began filtering through Manchester Airport on their way to Lisbon for a Champions League match that marks the next stop in what has turned into a desperate campaign.

The prevailing mood was one of resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour around what a season in the Championship might look like, and whether Manchester City might be there with them.

United's England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed the situation up when he spoke to MUTV after the final whistle at Anfield.

"We're at the lowest we've ever been and no-one's coming to save us," said the 21-year-old.

"There are no helping hands coming, so we've got to work together, lean on each other, keep working and hopefully it will come good.

"It's all about character now.".

Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half-year contract.

United are giving little away about their plans for the January transfer window.

For now, it is being stressed, Pochettino's priority is to get the most from the players currently at his disposal.

However, there was sympathy with former boss Michael Carrick's belief he had been let down in the summer window and there was a plan to address that.

That situation remains. A striker is thought to be Pochettino's priority given United's only recognised number nine, Benjamin Sesko, is out at least until January with a shin problem that has bothered him since March.

Sources indicate that united have a long-standing issue at left-back. First choice Luke Shaw missed his eighth successive game on Sunday and the only other orthodox left-back in senior ranks is England Under-20 international Harry Amass, who didn't even make the bench at Anfield.

However, Pochettino worked with Shaw at the start of his career at Southampton and feels the 31-year-old can be a positive influence on his group.

The reality though is United still have nine games to play before they can make any changes to their squad.

Among those fixtures are home games against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland.

Newly promoted Coventry are four points ahead of United, who are second from bottom. Forest and Sunderland are in the two positions immediately above the Old Trafford club.

A trip to Crystal Palace - the one side below United, and the other Premier League club to replace their coach during the international break - looms on 13 December.

After Wednesday's encounter with Sporting, Pochettino's side have one Champions League game before the end of the year - against RB Leipzig on 8 December.

Recent findings suggest that any solutions to be found to the current mess over the next five weeks have to come from within. If they don't, light-hearted discussions about a first relegation since 1973-74 under Tommy Docherty start to get serious.

"They have got enough in that squad to get themselves out of the bottom three," Ashley Young - a Premier League winner with United - told Match of the Day.

"They have not been showing that, but Pochettino has only just come in. He is going to want to get his team set up in a way that they are hard to beat. Right now, they do not look like they are hard to beat.

"It doesn't look like there is that togetherness. He has got to find a way to get that out of them. I am sure he will be able to do that when he has been longer in the job.".

Man Utd shouldn't worry about relegation right now - Young.

Pochettino shut down a question about United's terrible recent defensive record when he spoke to the media immediately after the game at Anfield.

"Tell me only about the circumstance today," he remarked. "I wasn't [here] in the past.".

That is true - and may also have been a useful diversion exercise in avoiding a dissection of a defensive unit he is still getting to know.

However, Pochettino knows United have kept one clean sheet all season - against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in September. He will also know United have now conceded 19 goals in their past six games.

Pochettino's major decision at Liverpool was to pick Matthijs de Ligt in the centre of a three-man defence ahead of Harry Maguire.

"He played in the Champions League you know, before the internationals," said the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss.

It was not clear when Pochettino meant.

Sources indicate that in the 4-1 loss at Como on 21 October, De Ligt made his first appearance in 11 months following major back problems that eventually required surgery, largely because Leny Yoro was suspended and Lisandro Martinez was injured. He then played for two minutes against Roma on 3 November, when he was thrown on as then manager Carrick searched desperately for a winner.

Most goals can be broken down into a number of mistakes that compound to make an eventual negative outcome.

Team positioning has been mentioned as a reason De Ligt found himself exposed under a high ball at Anfield. However, his failure to deal with it presented Alexander Isak with a clear run at goal and prompted Yoro to make the tackle that led to his controversial dismissal, which Pochettino felt shaped the 82 minutes that followed.

According to recent reports, but United have been conceding bad goals all season. Numerous players have been culpable.

There is a limit to what Pochettino can do in the time available. However, he wants to maximise what he can do.

Whereas Carrick tended to let his starting players have a day off after matches, the new regime has decided a warm-down session at Carrington is the better option.

And defensive organisation was surely one of the key points his coaching team had on their list of things to work on when the players began preparations to face Sporting on Wednesday.

Midfielder Andrey Santos has started three out of 10 Premier League games since the opening-day defeat at Hull.

With Â£70m summer arrival Carlos Baleba injured for the second time since the start of pre-season, Pochettino must find a way to protect United's goal, which might require additional support in midfield.

The strengths of Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are with the ball. Either with three in the middle of defence or a third man in midfield, a way needs to be found to stop opposition attacks running straight at the defence.

In his recent interview with Sky Sports, United chief executive Omar Berrada said the club needed to be "disciplined" in the transfer market and avoid spending huge sums on players who would not necessarily make the squad better.

But the fact former Chelsea midfielder Andrey Santos went five games between Premier League starts under Carrick from the opening-day defeat at Hull - and was only introduced for the final three minutes at Anfield - suggests there are doubts over the Brazilian, who cost Â£48m in the summer.

Underneath that is the knowledge United borrowed from their revolving credit facility around all their major summer purchases and did the same again earlier this month when Pochettino was hired at a cost of just over Â£7.5m.

In public accounts released last week, United confirmed there was another Â£160m available in credit - but also they owe Â£417m in outstanding transfer fees, Â£236m of which is due within 12 months.

Neither before nor after the transfer window opens do any simple solutions to United's predicament present themselves.

Last season, fellow 'big-six' club Tottenham did not save themselves until the final day of the season.

Confidence remains high at Old Trafford the situation will not be quite so dire for them, but it could be a very bumpy ride.

#150797. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (767 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal notable differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism demonstrated remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal notable differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

Industry observers note that to explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

Sources indicate that at first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism indicated substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

The results raise crucial questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Sources indicate that traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

In a recent development, the researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

  • Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.
  • Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in Newly introduced York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”.

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go.

According to recent reports, in the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.).

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

It has been revealed that criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.).

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.).

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”.

Trump's risky call for protests.

According to recent reports, greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”.

In a recent development, now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.).

Join us on Twitter and Facebook.

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”.

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy.
  • According to recent reports, researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words.
  • The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A upcoming study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

According to recent reports, researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," remarked Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy indicates up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction.".

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy.

According to recent reports, the researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about vital moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

According to recent reports, the analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language.

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, revealed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

According to recent reports, boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

Sources indicate that "What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life.".

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

In a recent development, this variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

In a recent development, "People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships.".

Industry observers note that like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

According to recent reports, this approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment.

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

Industry observers note that "That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's crucial to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict.".

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she remarked. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions.".

COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's intends to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.
  • But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's intends to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

Sources indicate that the IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this concern, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions.".

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action intends for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Sources indicate that disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," mentioned a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

According to recent reports, "We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive.".

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake.".

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science.".

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

It has been revealed that the IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the looks to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

In a recent development, at least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment.".

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

Sources indicate that the presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest massive-screen adventure

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
  • In a recent development, with the Borg overrunning the newly rolled out USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat.
  • But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend.

In a recent development, with the Borg overrunning the newly rolled out USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch.

But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive.

It has been revealed that it's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect.

And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath.

According to recent reports, in 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even numbers good" rule of "Trek" films still, more or less, rang true. 1994's "Generations", rushed out a few months after "The Next Generation" ended its seven-year run on TV, had done decent business, but the seventh movie's convoluted "passing the baton" storyline had left many fans cold. Now, however, with Kirk killed off, it was time for Picard and his crew to explore the big-screen frontier alone.

It has been revealed that william Shatner actually pitched a resurrection storyline for Kirk, but "Trek" executive producer/overlord Rick Berman ruled that it was a little too soon to bring the good captain back. Instead, he hired "Generations" scripters and "TNG"/"Deep Space Nine" writers' room regulars Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore to craft an eighth movie capable of living up to its even-numbered predecessors.

While "Generations" had been written to an extremely restrictive brief, Braga and Moore were given much more freedom the second time out. Berman was keen on a time-travel storyline while Braga lobbied for the fan-favorite Borg, and early on they explored the idea of taking the Collective back to Renaissance Italy. These looks were abandoned when Stewart vetoed the idea of wearing tights.

They eventually zeroed in on April 5, 2063, the date Zefram Cochrane (a character who'd previously appeared in Original Series episode "Metamorphosis") made humanity's first warp flight and put Earth on the radar of a passing Vulcan ship.

"We landed on the idea of what I called the 'Star Trek' nativity scene — the birth of 'Star Trek'," Braga said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A Altman and Edward Gross.

"The three wise Vulcans who arrive on Earth and step out of their ship for our first contact with an extraterrestrial species. And the Borg were going to prevent that from happening, which really struck a bullseye for me, because it would allow non-'Star Trek' people to understand why 'Star Trek' matters by putting the crew and the Borg back in that time frame. I thought it would appeal to a larger audience. 'Star Trek' itself was at stake, and that was super cool to me.".

Industry observers note that paramount reportedly flirted with significant-name directors like Ridley Scott ("Alien", "Blade Runner") and John McTiernan ("Predator", "Die Hard"), before settling on Jonathan Frakes. Although this would be Frakes' first movie, the man best known for playing Commander Riker had directed numerous "Trek" episodes. Berman believed that an understanding of the franchise's DNA was more important than big-screen experience.

The film wastes little time on exposition for "Trek" newbies, with just a short dream sequence to explain away Picard's history with the Borg. With a single Borg Cube on course for Earth, the Federation fleet mobilizes to fight them off. They're getting their asses well and truly kicked, too, until the Enterprise warps into the battle.

The Cube is ultimately destroyed but still manages to dispatch a Sphere, which uses chronometric particles to travel back to 2063 in order to assimilate Earth in the past. Picard has no choice but to follow them back to "repair whatever damage they've done".

They arrive in a post-World War III Montana, where Cochrane has constructed his prototype faster-than-light vessel, the Phoenix. Played by "Babe" star James Cromwell (who'd already guest-starred in a trio of "TNG" episodes), Cochrane is some way from the man future history has remembered: a hard-drinking womanizer more motivated by potential riches than the betterment of mankind. A man uncomfortable with the idea that a high school will one day bear his name.

Sources indicate that but as some of the crew work to repair the damage caused by the Sphere's bombing raid, there are bigger problems in orbit. Borg survivors have beamed on board the Enterprise and started assimilating the vessel and its crew.

Initial drafts of the script saw Riker leading the ship-based resistance while Picard remained on Earth, but — at Stewart's request — Braga and Moore flipped things round to bring the captain face-to-face with his nemesis. It proved to be a really smart move, as Stewart got to ditch his new-look Starfleet uniform and run around the Enterprise as a full-on action hero in a John McClane-style vest.

It has been revealed that these Borg had been given a multiplex upgrade, with massively improved prosthetics and latest extendable tendrils that injected nanoprobes to assimilate a victim from within. Frakes played up the horror aspects of the Collective, portraying them as a horde of mindless cybernetic zombies, while using "Alien" and "Aliens" as inspiration.

It has been revealed that "[Ridley Scott and James Cameron] made it clear that when it comes to villains, the more that's suggested, the scarier they are," Frakes explained. "I tried to get that with the Borg.".

The biggest change came at the head of the organization, where — at the suggestion of Paramount executive Jonathan Dolgen — "First Contact" introduced a previously unseen Borg Queen (brilliantly played by Alice Krige) to act as spokesperson for the Collective.

Sources indicate that bringing a singular entity to a civilisation built on the notion that there's no "I" in "team" was a controversial move, but it made perfect dramatic sense. Indeed, a legion of drones would have little chance of seducing Data, even if it was just for 0.68 seconds.

Sources indicate that "We wrestled with it quite a bit before we committed to [the Borg Queen's] character," Moore told Syfy Wire, "because it was a choice that was also antithetical to the idea of the Borg. The whole concept of these villains was that they were a collection, and that there were no individuals. And that's what made them the faceless, implacable 'resistance is futile' enemy. But it also limited how to deal with them dramatically because it meant that any scenes you always had to deal with this sort of collective voice. We decided that the story would be better if we had some individual to deal with.".

The Queen was also granted one of the greatest entrances in sci-fi history, as her head and torso were lowered into a robot body with a bit of help from Industrial Light & Magic.

Industry observers note that the Starfleet armada's assault on the Borg was similarly impressive and effectively a test run for "The Phantom Menace", as ILM's visual effects supervisor John Knoll pioneered the CG effects pipeline that would later become pivotal to the "Star Wars" prequels. It was also a brilliant excuse to introduce several new starship designs to the "Trek" canon.

It has been revealed that they're standout moments in a film that made the most of its comparatively puny budget of $45 million (reported). (For comparison, "Independence Day", which was released the same year — and also featured Brent Spiner — cost closer to $75 million.).

Industry observers note that as Moore later recalled in an interview with the Hollywood Reporter, "Paramount had their formula. They said that 'Star Trek' movies only make this amount of money. So, therefore, you can only have this amount of budget to make it. And, at that point, we were still — just like on the TV show — counting phaser beam effects shots [to keep the price down].".

Industry observers note that the studio needn't have worried. "First Contact" was a huge hit with fans and became one of the franchise's highest-grossing films at the box office. Borg mythology introduced here (including the Queen) would become a mainstay on "Star Trek: Voyager", while Jean-Luc would get to face his cybernetic white whale again in "Picard" — though the incomparable Stewart arguably never again had another "Trek" scene to rival the ones he had here.

Recent findings suggest that "Fortunately it happened to be a wonderful script, and my job was not to screw it up," noted Frakes. "It also holds up as a movie that just happens to be a 'Star Trek' movie, which we were all hoping would be the case.".

'Star Trek: First Contact' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

Industry observers note that richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.

Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.

There are some notable differences between each Workspace blueprint – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three prepares come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.

It has been revealed that google offers four different Workspace looks, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.

Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the initiative you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard prepares. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

Gemini is also a substantial difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That highlights up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this strategy, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

According to recent reports, most people should use the Standard blueprint, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

In a recent development, google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., revision a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.

You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.

Sources indicate that let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.

Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make prepares, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.

#150787. A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal upcoming physics

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1613 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal upcoming physics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover.
  • In a recent development, the mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
  • Recent findings suggest that when the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

In a recent development, the mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

Recent findings suggest that when the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

Sources indicate that there is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors.

Industry observers note that previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

In a recent development, unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

In a recent development, the UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

It has been revealed that if cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

Sources indicate that "The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," remarked Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as newly introduced physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted.".

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data.

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an vital independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

It has been revealed that the latest approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

According to recent reports, to demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it demonstrates that the latest method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe.

The technique could also play an key role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

Recent findings suggest that E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

Industry observers note that one known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter.

Sources indicate that the challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

According to recent reports, the UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement.".

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy.

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

According to recent reports, although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most key unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

In a recent development, one possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely fresh way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those at the moment understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI was released on consoles last week, with millions of players exploring Leonida on Xbox and PS5 consoles. But one major question remains: What's happening with the online mode?

The GTA Online component of Grand Theft Auto V has kept that 13-year-old game relevant across three console generations, with a recent leak suggesting Rockstar makes as much as $500 million annually from microtransactions alone. One would think that means GTA VI will have a similar online offering available at launch, but that isn't the case. Per a Rockstar statement given to IGN, as well as all available marketing language on digital storefronts, GTA VI is a "single-player experience.".

There was no online component at launch, nor has Rockstar confirmed any intention of adding one after launch. Sadly, that is all the concrete information anyone can provide right now.

However, that doesn't mean all hope is lost. It's worth remembering that both GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2 released as solo experiences and got online modes later, though it was only a matter of months in both cases. Given that Rockstar hasn't even said if there will be a fresh GTA Online experience for VI, it's probably safe to assume the wait will be longer this time.

In a recent development, the fact that the existing GTA Online is so wildly successful (with no signs of slowing down) means Rockstar isn't necessarily incentivized to make a new one right away. It also means Rockstar has to decide if it wants to keep two different GTA Online experiences running at the same time, should GTA VI ever get one. As IGN noted, Grand Theft Auto publisher Take-Two right now supports two different NBA 2K Online games in the Asian market; the first rolled out in 2012 and its sequel in 2017, but they're both popular enough to coexist to this day.

Unfortunately, we don't have a definitive answer on when we'll get a new GTA Online mode tied to the new game, but hey, single-player games aren't so bad. I'm sure there will be plenty of hours of entertainment to be had in GTA VI as it is.

Does your Monday morning WFH routine need an immediate morale boost before Thanksgiving travel chaos completely derails your week? Krispy Kreme is quietly running a free promotion that's worth the detour.

NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange fresh world

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising latest perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.
  • On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system.
  • It has been revealed that the image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising latest perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

It has been revealed that the image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos.

It has been revealed that "The first thing we noted was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole latest world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges.".

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

Sources indicate that when DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an key part of Hera's investigation.

According to recent reports, ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.".

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit.

Sources indicate that although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's fresh image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

Recent findings suggest that NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact.

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

Sources indicate that while DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

Sources indicate that "Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!".

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Sources indicate that materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Industry News: What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 2 min read (458 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.
  • The group known as OPEC+ unveiled Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year.
  • The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more rapidly than the spike in oil prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ unveiled Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more rapidly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” mentioned Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”.

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza noted he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he stated. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts.

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US intends additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he mentioned.

#150776. The Manosphere Isn’t Ready for Brothercore

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4081 w)
