Tech Report: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means.
  • The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations.
  • "What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," claims Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. New research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," claims Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

Members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

These contrasting perspectives may have crucial consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to newly introduced evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science.

Dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

The researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

Both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

In a recent development, some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as latest challenges arise.

Sources indicate that dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Why the Public Sees Science Differently.

In a recent development, another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

One possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

Recent findings suggest that the differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when fresh evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery.

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

With researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

The study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

According to recent reports, "Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she indicates. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.".

#150656. Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty.
  • A new study suggests they become more likely to follow.
  • In a recent development, A small number did more than copy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

In a recent development, A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group.".

Sources indicate that the researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Recent findings suggest that participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Sources indicate that each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

In a recent development, small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

According to recent reports, good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

Recent findings suggest that people also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

It has been revealed that to see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

Molleman calls the work fundamental science and notes the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

Recent findings suggest that he also notes it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.".

According to recent reports, the must-have gadget for women of almost any age is an LED mask. These masks promise to use red light to erase wrinkles, brighten your skin, and keep acne at bay. I haven't seen much change in my wrinkles in my year-plus of regularly using a red-light mask, but I can confirm it makes my skin brighter and calms down acne and scars much faster when I'm regularly treating my skin, and I always get compliments on how nice my skin looks when I'm regularly using it. According to recent reports, look, nothing says mom life like looking for the perfect bag. I'm in a massive tote phase of my life; I somehow need to either lug an armload of items for myself and my son (or just myself!) or I only need a tiny belt bag. There's no in between.

To me, motherhood is all about change. It's most obvious at the start of motherhood, when your body changes a lot over the course of nine months, but motherhood encompasses the rest of our lives, and our bodies and style change a lot over that time. One of the biggest giveaways that time has gone by is our clothes—how well they fit for our current stage, whether they reflect the time of our life right now, and if we're bored out of our skull with everything but don't want to buy an entirely new closet.

Former Netflix chief content officer Bela Bajaria addressed her exit from the streamer in her first public comments about her abrupt departure last month.

Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the 2026 International Emmys, where she’s set to be honored with the Founders Award, Bajaria called her decade at Netflix “such an amazing, fun chapter” and shared she was “proud of so many of the things” that she and her team had accomplished.

Since her exit, Bajaria said she’s been indulging in “a little rest” and having some “really fun conversations.” Related Stories Movies Sadie Sandler to Star in Netflix Horror Movie 'Malibu' From Vertigo, Happy Madison (Exclusive) Movies 'The Odyssey' Leads Critics Choice Awards Below-The-Line Shortlists.

“I’m excited about what’s next, and I think this time is good for a little rest after a lot of global travel,” she told THR on the red carpet ahead of the awards show, adding that she’s “really open” to whatever the future holds.

Bajaria was ousted from her role at Netflix on Oct. 15, with former Fox and Disney exec Peter Rice taking her place as chief content officer.

The former chief content officer previously spoke with THR at the Saban Community Clinic Gala at the end of October but wasn’t yet ready to speak about her time at Netflix. Still she offered, “the outpouring that I’ve received in the last couple of weeks has been so beautiful and amazing. I’ve been in television for 30 years, and at this point I have worked with what feels like nearly every single person from agents and producers to writers and actors. I love it. I’m so grateful for the career I have had to date, with lots more to come.”.

Speaking to THR at the International Emmys, Bajaria also weighed in on the recent departures of a number of top female executives amid ongoing layoffs and restructuring efforts, including Pam Abdy at Warner Bros. and Cindy Holland at Paramount.

“I think in general, in every industry, we just have to make sure that you have leaders that are doing a great job and really care about the group and are making those decisions,” Bajaria said. “And it matters who’s in those roles, and I think we should always just be aware of that.”.

She added that it was particularly notable to think of who’s in leadership roles and making decisions and “people’s backgrounds” when you’re “greenlighting” movies and TV shows.

Still she’s looking back on her time at Netflix with gratitude and excitement for what’s next.

It has been revealed that “I’m so proud of being part of something that transforms television and film and connecting with audiences around the world,” she told THR. “I’m just really excited to be here to celebrate a long career at this point and that’s really what it’s about. Let’s see what’s next.”.

Bajaria, who joined Netflix after serving as president of Universal Television at NBCUniversal, left the streamer as it shed 1,000 employees, roughly six percent of its workforce, including execs Doug Belgrad and, days after news broke of Bajaria leaving, film boss Dan Lin. The layoffs came as the manufacturer seeks a reset amid slowing viewership growth.

When she left Netflix, co-CEO Ted Sarandos stated of Bajaria, “Bela has built and shaped a truly global Content organization, hiring brilliant people and empowering them to make good decisions. I am incredibly grateful to her for everything she’s done.”.

He added in a staff memo, “I know this is a big change in a year that has already had its share. But I also see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in [the U.S. and Canada] where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world.”.

Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.
  • Industry observers note that the limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD.
  • Sources indicate that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.

Industry observers note that the limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD. However, a large Latin cross carved into its lid dates to approximately the 10th or 11th century, suggesting that the person buried inside lived hundreds of years after the coffin was originally made.

Sources indicate that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation. The remains likely belong to a prominent medieval monk, and researchers have narrowed the possible identities to two men who once led Westminster Abbey.

Two Medieval Abbots Emerge as Leading Candidates.

The newly introduced findings, published in the peer-reviewed Journal of the British Archaeological Association, come from Professor Warwick Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Rodwell identifies Aelfwig, an abbot who died around 1020, as the strongest candidate. At the time, Westminster Abbey was a Benedictine monastery, and Aelfwig had served there as a monk before becoming its abbot.

Another possibility is Wulnoth, who succeeded Aelfwig and died in 1049. Both men are believed to have been buried at the Abbey, making either a plausible match for the skeleton.

"We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," says Professor Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Recent findings suggest that "We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to fifty when he died.

"The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.".

The elaborate burial provides another reason to suspect that the deceased held an crucial position. Rodwell suggests that the individual was 'honored' with a 'fine sarcophagus', an unusual distinction that would be consistent with the status of an abbot.

Rather than commissioning an entirely new stone coffin, those responsible for the burial apparently reused an existing Roman sarcophagus. The man's wooden coffin was placed inside it, and the stone lid was modified with a prominent Latin cross. This may represent an early example of recycling a valuable object for an entirely different purpose.

New Excavations Reveal the Skeleton's Age.

According to recent reports, the Roman sarcophagus and its mysterious occupant have fascinated researchers for generations. Rodwell's latest conclusions draw on several investigations conducted with specialists over the years, including work associated with Channel 4's Time Team.

In 2009, the television program examined the archaeology and architecture of King Henry III's original sacristy, located along the north side of Westminster Abbey.

The same area was the scene of an earlier accidental discovery in 1820, when workers encountered the Roman coffin and broke its lid into six pieces. The damage was repaired around the time the sarcophagus was formally 'discovered' in 1869.

More recently, Pre-Construct Archaeology, one of the UK's largest commercial archaeological and heritage organizations, carried out another excavation of the sacristy. Completed in 2025, the project was undertaken to support construction of the King Charles III Sacristy, a new facility at Westminster Abbey scheduled to open the following year.

As part of this investigation, human bone specialist James Young Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology (PCA) conducted a fresh examination of the skeleton.

Recent findings suggest that his analysis indicated that the deceased was a man between 35 and 49 years old who stood approximately 5 feet 9 inches tall. These findings differ considerably from an assessment made in the 1800s, which described the remains as those of a 'robust young man' no older than 30 and approximately 5 feet 7 inches tall.

Carbon Dating Confirms a 1,000-Year-Old Burial.

One of the most crucial clues came from scientific dating of the remains. A bone sample was submitted to the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre for radiocarbon analysis, which produced a date range of 987 to 1052 AD.

It has been revealed that this places the burial firmly within the late Saxon period, centuries after the Roman sarcophagus was originally created. The dates also align with the deaths of both Aelfwig and Wulnoth, strengthening the case that the skeleton belonged to one of these medieval abbots.

"This confirms that the reuse of the sarcophagus, and the associated remodeling of its cover, occurred in the late Saxon period.".

The results provide scientific support for the theory that an ancient Roman burial container was repurposed to honor an key religious figure nearly 1,000 years ago.

A Skeleton Thought Lost Was Hiding in Plain Sight.

Sources indicate that the investigation also brought renewed attention to an unexpected discovery made in 2016. For years, researchers had believed that the skeleton was missing, leaving an important part of the burial's history unresolved.

That assumption proved mistaken when the sarcophagus was transported to a conservation studio. PCA researchers removed its lid and were surprised to find an almost complete human skeleton still inside.

It has been revealed that the examination produced another clue that Rodwell describes as a 'remarkable new discovery'. Inside the stone coffin, researchers identified the rectangular outline of a structure that had disappeared long ago. Its shape was preserved by a white residue left behind by lime, a material historically used in burials.

Rodwell believes the outline marks the position of the original wooden coffin that held the deceased before it was placed inside the Roman sarcophagus.

"Although no physical traces of that feature remained, it can only have been a timber coffin, which has completely decayed over the course of the seven centuries that the sarcophagus was buried in the sacristy courtyard," writes Professor Rodwell.

Recent findings suggest that together, the rediscovered skeleton, evidence of a wooden coffin, and upcoming scientific dating have transformed researchers' understanding of this unusual burial. Although the man's identity has not been established beyond doubt, the findings suggest that a medieval abbot may have been laid to rest in a Roman coffin already centuries old.

Visitors can see the sarcophagus today in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet.
  • The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible upcoming imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus.
  • This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet.

The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible upcoming imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus.

This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera.

Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains.

In a recent development, despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers).

In a recent development, while Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported.

In addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material.

The observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past.

By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic.

Recent findings suggest that after word hit the street some days back that Vanity Fair was imminently going to publish an extensively reported hit piece on music’s biggest superstar, there was some anticipation that Monday might turn out to be a bad day for Taylor Swift. Instead, it was just a bad day for journalism. As attention-seeking magazine articles go, it’s hard to remember one that landed with quite such an unanticipated — but very loud — thud as “The Mastermind,” which has even hardened anti-Swifties wondering whether May Jeong slipped it through without editorial oversight, sneaking an alleged year’s worth of work onto the internet in the dead of morning.

In a recent development, the alternative scenario was unthinkable. You would have to imagine that the author had actually been encouraged by editors to puzzle readers with a reported op-ed in which the subject of the piece — apparently, some top-tier celebrity! — is never named, yet still is subject to accusations that she picks her own friends, harbors ambitions, owned three pairs of Ugg boots while posing as a teenage commoner, and, most slanderously, was actually popular in school.

It has been revealed that when was the last time a high-profile magazine piece got ratio-ed this badly? That would have been one year and one week ago, when an exclusive excerpt from Olivia Nuzzi’s memoir, “American Canto,” was released to an incredulous world. And if there’s something that feels a little bit familiar about Jeong’s oddball tactic of not naming names in her piece (or at least not the big ones), it’s because this “you know who it’s about, but we’re not gonna say anyway” technique was a weird conceit last grafted into big-time American journalism by Nuzzi. That author referred to RFK only as “the Politician,” her ex-boyfriend as “the man I did not marry,” and so on. Nuzzi walked so that Jeong could run. Although this upcoming piece is not any kind of roman a clef, she still feels compelled to euphemize Swift as “The Star,” her former label as “The Machine,” Scooter Braun as “The Manager,” Charli xcx as “The Brat” and even a secondary source as “The Person Familiar.”.

Sources indicate that you would think Vanity Fair’s editors would recall the horrible reviews Nuzzi got for employing this gambit in “American Canto,” especially since the excerpt that introduced that annoying running gag to the world was published in… Vanity Fair. (How swiftly they forget, but monthly journalism is a grind.).

The article aims to unload secrets, but the secret we really need revealed is: Why do that? An interview with Jeong is in order. Or perhaps she is saving the rationale for her journalism class at Princeton, which may be the only one destined to have “The Mastermind” as ciriculum. On first blush, a journalism non-pro might imagine that it was done to skirt libel laws, although that explanation holds no water, since the writer does quote several of her lowest-level sources by name, like the kids from Swift’s school who are ready to call her out now for not having been friendless or unmoneyed. (The former classmates will pick up some notoriety now, but will they regret that they could have become even more legendary if they’d been ID-ed as “The Girl Who Noticed The Star’s Uggs”?) No, it seems more likely that Jeong did it because we are, all of us, just archetypes in a fable. Except for the music teacher at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High, who is un-archetypical enough to require a first and last name. Related Stories Meghan Markle’s Father Arrested Over Allegations He Possessed Child Sex Abuse Images AI Films From Kerala to the Andaman Islands Set for WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon, Screen at IFFI Goa (EXCLUSIVE).

According to recent reports, or perhaps Jeong refrains from naming Swift because she is the female equivalent of two other characters who are often referred to as He Who Must Not Be Named: Voldemort and Trump. Certainly the article seems to see Swift as an exemplor of the banality of evil, or, more to the point, a modern-day, real-life Regina George from “Mean Girls.” (No, not making that up, the journalist really goes with that.) Nearly every sentence is intended as a slap. Most journos writing a piece remotely in this vein — a reported one, as opposed to a straight opinion column — would try to leaven it at least once or twice with a positive or just neutral observation, before dropping the next bomb. “The Mastermind,” to its honest credit, dispenses with any such “See, I went into this with an open mind” niceties.

According to recent reports, the Star is found by The Writer to be “making herself a metonym for all women, successfully equat(ing) criticism against her as criticism against womenkind.” Compared to Katy Perry (aka “The California Girl”), who is “an adult pretending to be a child,” Swift “might be a child pretending to be an adult.” She “has a reputation for being punitive. She seems too invested in her own victimhood.” For Swift, “all she had ever wanted from the world was that it celebrate her milky goodness, that her altruism not be mistaken for covert narcissism.” And then from there, Jeong gets to some of Swift’s bad qualities. (Just kidding.).

Sources indicate that if this were framed in any way as a commentary, as opposed to Vanity Fair objectively speaking in the voice of God, it wouldn’t catch much notice. But instead, the magazine frames it as an ultimate profile, the result of a year of work and talking to “over 100 sources.” We have to take the editors’ word for that, because the reportage as printed only quotes six sources on the record: the mother of a man who directed Swift in her school plays, a guitar teacher, a school music teacher, two girls who sat near Swift in music class, and a poet who is called in to assess how lyrics work. Five others are quoted anonymously: someone who used to be close to Swift, called The Person Familiar; a music pro called The Exec; a mystery ex-collaborator whose profession must be kept secret; a musician who toured with Swift; and a critic who was ostracized after slamming her… none of whom, even under the cloak of keeping their identities secret, have serious tea to spill. Now, reporters do often get great background information from interviews they don’t quote, so the 100-plus figure doesn’t sound completely unrealistic after so many months of reporting. But if these dozen or so sources were the best that the story had to actually quote — including a poet and a critic — you do have to wonder who the other 85-plus were, to be less quotable. (An editor’s introduction to the piece notes one of the people interviewed was a “lover” of Swift’s, but we’ll just have to guess if the writer got to Joe Alwyn.).

It has been revealed that all that remarked, there are a handful of interesting questions and critical observations scattered through Jeong’s piece. (See? This is the part where you throw in something nice, to show you were objective.) If you removed the promise of fact-finding and this existed as an essay on Salon — RIP — you could credit her with some food-for-thought lines and decently amusing zingers. (Sure, I chuckled when Jeong, alluding to Travis Kelce, wrote, “Regretfully we must call him Redwood.”).

But the veneer of investigative reporting placed upon this piece mostly indicates just how low the bar is for an attempted expose anymore. Even without the terminally twee names. It’d be nice to suppose that Jeong really did come up with something after a year — there is so much hinted at that is quickly dropped — and that Vanity Fair’s lawyers gutted a more substantial piece to within an inch of a life. But more probably, it’s an example of snark masquerading as reportage. And it shows again that some journalists (even journalists that teach at Princeton) are too quick, when an expensive. exhaustive fishing expedition fails to turn up much, to succumb to a sad maxim: If you can’t get the goods, just get cute. But don’t expect readers who expect more out of their hit squads not to notice.

Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.

The retailer remarked its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

It has been revealed that encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

"The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time.".

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the tech giant performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

According to recent reports, for the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

This year, the organization remarked it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

It has been revealed that the company noted it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

Recent findings suggest that the massive-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and stated it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.

It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer stated on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.

Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

The Hunger Games franchise has whetted appetites for more films, given the success of its latest title.

Recent findings suggest that lionsgate released The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping over the weekend, with the movie grossing a commanding $119.3 million from 4,018 North American locations to open in first place at the box office. The feature adaptation of author Suzanne Collins‘ 2025 prequel novel notched a better opening frame than the two most recent entries in the six-film series that kicked off with 2012’s Jennifer Lawrence-led The Hunger Games. Related Stories Movies 'You Can See Everything' Crosses $100M Globally, Becomes First Doc to Hit 1M Letterboxd Watches Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up.

In a recent development, during a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter to celebrate the success of Sunrise on the Reaping, Lionsgate Motion Picture Group chair Adam Fogelson emphasizes that the studio would love to collaborate again with Collins on another project in the franchise. Director Francis Lawrence‘s latest movie stars Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, portrayed in the first four films by Woody Harrelson. The $150 million-budgeted feature is set 24 years before the events of Collins’ original 2008 book.

“We have complete respect for Suzanne as the architect,” Fogelson indicates. “I have told her that, if and when she is ready for me to read something else, I will drop everything and go anywhere in the world to get to read it. And I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had a far bigger impact at the box office than the 2023 prequel film The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which starred Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer. Centering on the backstory for villainous President Snow — portrayed in the newly introduced movie by Ralph Fiennes — Songbirds and Snakes opened to $44 million domestically before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million.

Sources indicate that “All of us understood that the story that Suzanne wanted to tell on Songbirds was a challenging one and that she was inspired to tell it,” Fogelson explains. “She did it in an extraordinary way. Clearly, the movie worked really well for the audience that saw it, but the origin story of the villain — with no grand Hunger Games spectacle at the center of the story — is a challenging ask.”.

He continues, “But we are in very regular, very authentic dialogue with this giant fan base, and we had plenty of indications that a story like this one could relight the fire in an exceptional way. It’s why we chose to invest the way that we did, both in the production plan and in the casting. And so, we were confident that there were plenty of signals that, if you gave the audience a story like this one, they were ready to return in big numbers.”.

In a recent development, as far as what a potential sequel movie could entail, Fogelson notes that the franchise’s supporters have offered suggestions about potentially fertile storytelling opportunities within the dystopian world. The Sunrise on the Reaping book sold 1.5 million copies in its first week, making it the biggest launch among Collins’ titles in the series.

“The fan base have definitely let us all know that there are other stories they would be thrilled to both read and watch,” states Fogelson. “We’ll see if any of them spark Suzanne to go ahead and write them.”.

The exec pointed out that each major character reveal during the film’s Upcoming York premiere was met with feverish cheers from the audience. The new movie’s expansive cast includes Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke and Whitney Peak.

Industry observers note that “It starts with the fact that Suzanne decided to tell a story that the audience had clearly been desperate for — anchored by a character that the audience both loved and was fascinated to learn more about — and then the filmmaking team and the production group at the studio partnered to cast and make an exceptional version of that story,” Fogelson claims. “This is one of the most exceptionally put-together casts I’ve ever been a part of.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal President’s latest major trip takes him to Africa. Frank-Walter Steinmeier has just visited the Ivory Coast and is continuing on to Ghana and Kenya. His goal: to encourage more German companies to invest in Africa.

Frank-Walter Steinmeier has visited 31 African countries during his political career. Even as foreign minister, he traveled regularly to the continent; as federal president, he has made twelve trips so far.

In a recent development, from early on, he viewed Africa not only through the lens of development aid and humanitarian support, but also — much like former Chancellor Angela Merkel — as a market for the German economy that has been underutilized thus far. In 2015, as foreign minister in the Merkel administration, Steinmeier played a central role in the creation of the German-African Economic Summit.

On his current trip as well, Steinmeier is advocating for greater German engagement in Africa. In Abidjan, the capital of the Ivory Coast, following a meeting with Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara, he called on German companies to step outside their comfort zone and take greater advantage of the opportunities offered by the country and the continent.

The Ivory Coast is considered a location with growing potential. Despite its proximity to the Sahel region, which is plagued by terrorism, the country is relatively stable politically. The economy is growing by about six percent annually. Germany has more intensive trade relations with the Ivory Coast than with any other country in sub-Saharan Africa, and nowhere else in sub-Saharan Africa do so many people learn German — an advantage for German small and medium-sized enterprises — all of which both presidents emphasized very clearly during their meeting in Abidjan.

Recent findings suggest that up next, Steinmeier is scheduled to visit Accra, Ghana, for the sixth German-African Economic Summit, where more than 600 business representatives are expected to attend. As the summit’s initiator, the Federal President will open the event together with the host, Ghanaian President John Mahama. He will be accompanied by a ten-member business delegation representing industry, the financial sector, and energy consulting.

According to recent reports, the Economic Summit is taking place at a time when Germany’s relations with African countries are undergoing fundamental changes. In light of geopolitical shifts, Africa is increasingly coming into focus as an economic and trade partner.

In a recent development, the continent’s share of German foreign trade presently stands at just under 2%, or around €30 billion. At the same time, German exports to Africa are rising by at least 6% annually. And since Germany’s economy aims to reduce its dependence on China in the future, opportunities in Africa are growing.

From Ghana, Frank-Walter Steinmeier will travel on to Kenya, the final stop on his tour of Africa.

A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics,  AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.

The study also showed about 300 new deep tech startups are expected to be founded this year, a 40% rise compared with last year.

Newly found startups tend to be founded around economic hubs like Berlin and Hamburg, which are also home to leading universities and research institutes.

The study also highlighted challenges, including limited funding compared with their US counterparts and insufficient support to move startups from the laboratory to the real world.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools.".

Read more about the disruptive incidents that have targeted Europe in recent weeks.

Germany's Freie Wähler (Free Voters) party have chosen a newly introduced chairman, weeks after their former front man Hubert Aiwanger unexpectedly passed away on November 4.

It has been revealed that the party announced on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. The second state co-chair still needs to be decided.

Recent findings suggest that aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria.

Sources indicate that the Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

There are also changes in the Bavarian state government. Tobias Gotthardt is to take over as economy minister, while Environment Minister Thorsten Glauber is set to become deputy premier behind Bavaria state Premier Markus Söder. The appointments still require formal approval by party conventions.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has inisted that NATO was ready to defend itself in the face of potential Russian threats against any of its member states.

"We will always defend every inch of our NATO territory," Wadephul mentioned at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

His comments come after three Russian projectiles violated Polish airspace on Friday and crashed in the southeast of the country.

Wadephul is attending the NATO assembly in Berlin and DW has   a dedicated blog on those talks  where you can read all about how Russia's war in Ukraine is taking center stage for the defense alliance.

Industry observers note that A massive strike is underway in Germany hitting major car brands another manufacturing factors. Metal and electrical workers are demanding better pay ahead of upcoming wage talks later this week. The strike has been initiated by IG Metall, Germany’s biggest and most powerful union.

Famous car brands Mercedes and BMW  were affected as was an Opel plant, which is part of the international Stellantis group.

Recent findings suggest that the strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.

The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.

The tough struggle over wages comes as especially the German car industry is facing serious headwinds because of higher energy prices, US tariffs and mounting Chinese competition.

A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.

The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it indicates was circulated at the start of November.

It said that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.

The report stated the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.

German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin stated the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.

The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.

This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.

Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.

Sources indicate that german exports to Africa have reached a latest record. That’s according to a fresh study just as the country's president embarks on a trip to several African countries.

Exports are expected to rise by 6% in 2026 to reach about 30 billion euros ($33bn).

What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.

Industry observers note that the biggest single export at the moment is a high-speed train network to Egypt. Other main exports include electrical equipment, optical instruments, plastics and pharmaceuticals, as well as food products, including dairy goods, cereals and baked goods.

The data is being reported by the Reuters news agency, based on the government-owned agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI), which promotes foreign trade and investment in Germany.

In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.

The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.

"The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.

Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.

Major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention plans to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.

"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.

The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.

He begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.

In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa.".

His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.

The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.

The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.

Police are investigating a suspected case of aggravated arson after a fire broke out at a hospital in Berlin.

Investigators believe a patient set fire to his bed in a room on the first floor of one of the hospital buildings in the Lichtenberg district on Sunday evening.

One nurse and the suspected arsonist suffered smoke inhalation and had to be treated in hospital. Overall, 15 people were injured with another 13 suffering from minor injuries.

While firefighters managed to put out the flames, smoke spread to other parts of the hospital which then had to be evacuated.

#150644. Breaking: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

Breaking: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole.
  • Sources indicate that the center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment.
  • Sources indicate that over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole. An international research team led by MPE has traced these compact clouds to a massive pair of stars whose powerful winds appear to produce material that could eventually help feed the black hole, known as Sagittarius A*.

Sources indicate that the center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment. At its core sits Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), a supermassive black hole surrounded by stars, gas, and dust moving through a region dominated by intense gravitational forces. This extreme setting gives astronomers an opportunity to investigate how matter moves near black holes and where the material that sustains their activity comes from.

Sources indicate that over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*. These mysterious "clumps" may provide vital clues about how material makes its way toward the black hole. However, scientists have struggled to determine where the clouds originate and what causes them to form.

Mysterious Gas Clouds Near the Milky Way's Black Hole.

One of the first major discoveries came in 2012, when astronomers identified a compact cloud of ionized gas called G2. Containing several times Earth's mass, the cloud produces emissions from hydrogen and helium, consistent with hot gas mixed with dust. It follows a highly elongated orbit around Sagittarius A* and has a faint extension trailing behind it, known as G2t.

According to recent reports, soon afterward, researchers examining older observations recognized another similar object, G1, traveling along a closely related path. The similarities suggested that G1, G2, and G2t might not be independent objects. Instead, they could represent concentrations of gas within a larger, continuous stream.

Even relatively small differences in gas density can make such a stream appear broken into separate clouds. This happens because the brightness of the gas increases in proportion to the square of its density, making denser regions stand out much more strongly.

More recently, astronomers observed gas in G2's trailing material gathering into another compact cloud that follows a similar orbit. Although this newly formed object might naturally be called G3, that designation had already been assigned to a different object. Together, the related clouds trace a connected flow of material through the Galactic Center, known as the G1-2-3 streamer.

According to recent reports, these clouds could play a surprisingly vital role in sustaining the black hole. Calculations suggest that if approximately one Earth mass of gas reaches Sagittarius A* every ten years, it could provide enough fuel to maintain the black hole's current level of activity. Discovering how the clouds form could therefore help explain how the black hole receives its supply of matter.

Astronomers Trace the Gas Clouds to Their Source.

Researchers have considered several possible explanations for the clouds, including powerful winds from massive stars, stellar explosions such as novae, and gas pulled away from objects by the black hole's gravity.

Sources indicate that to investigate, the MPE-led team used two advanced infrared spectrographs, SINFONI and ERIS. Both instruments employ adaptive optics to produce sharper observations. By examining a specific hydrogen emission feature called the Brackett‑γ line, the astronomers measured the clouds' positions and velocities and reconstructed their paths around Sagittarius A*.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a striking pattern. G1, G2, and G2t all follow orbits with nearly the same shape and orientation. It would be extraordinarily unlikely for three unrelated clouds to share such closely matching orbital characteristics, strongly suggesting that they originated from the same source.

Two Massive Stars May Be Creating the Clouds.

By working backward from the clouds' observed motions and their velocities along our line of sight, the researchers identified a promising source: IRS 16SW, a massive contact binary system consisting of two stars in extremely close proximity.

The stellar pair belongs to a disk of young stars that revolves clockwise around Sagittarius A*. Its location and motion provide a plausible explanation for the gas stream. Even the slight differences between the clouds' orbital paths can be accounted for by the movement of the two stars around one another.

Computer simulations of how gas flows and interacts provided additional support for this explanation. The models indicate that powerful stellar winds from the binary system can collide with surrounding material, creating a shock in the region between the stars. Gas then accumulates and becomes compressed, forming dense concentrations that can eventually separate from the system.

Once released, these compact clouds can travel inward along paths resembling those observed in the G1-2-3 streamer. This provides a physical explanation for how one binary star system could produce several distinct clouds moving along closely related orbits.

A Newly introduced Clue to How Supermassive Black Holes Are Fed.

The findings suggest that massive stars near the Galactic Center may provide a continuing supply of gas capable of fueling Sagittarius A*. Rather than relying only on material already circulating around the black hole, the system could receive fresh gas from the powerful winds generated by nearby stars.

It has been revealed that the discovery also brings together several crucial processes in astronomy. The evolution of massive stars, the movement and compression of gas, and the supply of material to supermassive black holes may all be closely connected. By identifying a possible source of the mysterious clouds near Sagittarius A*, researchers have uncovered a new way in which stars could help sustain black hole activity at the heart of our own galaxy.
